When RAM fills up, the kernel can move rarely used memory pages to swap on disk. That keeps programs alive, but reading a page back from disk takes hundreds to thousands of times longer than from RAM, so a machine that swaps heavily turns sluggish and an engine's replies stall.

Think of a storage unit across town: it takes your overflow, but every trip there is slow. A little swap in use is normal. The console warns when more than half of the swap is used, which means the machine is short of memory and something should be stopped. Swap does not extend GPU memory.

temperature.title: Temperature
temperature.short: A setting for how random the model's word choices are, where 0 is the most predictable and higher is more varied.
temperature.long:
At each step the model gives every possible next token a probability, and temperature reshapes them before one is picked. Picture a dial from 'always order your usual' to 'surprise me'.

At 0 the engine always takes the most likely token, so the same prompt gives nearly the same answer, which suits code, data extraction and testing. Around 0.6 to 0.8 gives natural, varied chat. Above 1 answers get steadily more unpredictable. Many models publish a recommended temperature on their model card; follow it, especially for reasoning models, which can loop or ramble at 0.

tensor_parallelism.title: Tensor parallelism (TP)
tensor_parallelism.short: Splitting each layer of one model across several GPUs, so they all work on every token together.
tensor_parallelism.long:
With tensor parallelism of 2, every big matrix in each layer is cut in half, one half per card. Each token still passes through every layer, but each card does half of the work in each. That lets a model that does not fit one card run on two, and it speeds up each token (not always by 2x).

Think of two people carrying a heavy table: each takes half the weight, but they must move in step. The cost: after each layer the cards must exchange partial results, which needs fast links. With NVLink that is cheap. Over plain PCIe it takes a real bite out of the speed. The TP size must divide the model's number of attention heads, and the cards should be of similar size.

tensor_split.title: Tensor split (llama.cpp)
tensor_split.short: The proportions in which llama.cpp divides a model between several GPUs, such as 1,1 for equal halves.
tensor_split.long: With two cards, '1,1' puts half of the model on each, and '3,1' puts three quarters on the first. Use it when the cards have different amounts of free memory, or when one card also drives a display or runs another engine. The proportions decide how much of the model each card holds. They do not take the cards' speed into account. Without them, llama.cpp chooses a split itself. If one card runs out of memory while the other has space, shift the ratio towards the roomier card.

tensorrt_llm.title: TensorRT-LLM
tensorrt_llm.short: NVIDIA's engine for serving language models on NVIDIA GPUs only, tuned for speed on supported models.
tensorrt_llm.long: TensorRT-LLM is NVIDIA's own library. It optimises a model for NVIDIA hardware, including the newest number formats, and offers an OpenAI-compatible server. It runs on NVIDIA GPUs only. Model support and setup steps differ from the general-purpose engines, and its images are tied to specific CUDA and driver versions, so check that your model and your driver are supported before you choose it.

throughput.title: Throughput
throughput.short: How much work the engine gets done per second in total, usually tokens per second across all users.
throughput.long: Throughput and latency are two views of speed. Latency is how long one request takes. Throughput is how many tokens per second all requests together produce. They pull against each other: grouping more requests raises the total but makes each one a little slower. Chat wants low latency. Bulk jobs such as summaries or evaluations want high throughput. When you compare numbers, check whether they are per user or in total.

token.title: Token
token.short: The small piece of text a model reads and writes, which in English is about three-quarters of a word.
token.long: Models do not see letters or words. They see tokens: chunks of text such as 'the', ' under' or 'ing'. In English one token is roughly 4 characters or three-quarters of a word, so 1,000 tokens is about 750 words, or one and a half pages. Other languages, code and numbers often need more tokens per word. Everything is counted in tokens: the context window, the KV cache, the speed (tokens per second) and the usage statistics.

tokenizer.title: Tokenizer
tokenizer.short: The part that cuts text into tokens and glues tokens back into text, with a different one for every model family.
tokenizer.long:
A tokenizer holds a fixed vocabulary of pieces, from about 30,000 to over 250,000 of them, and the rules for splitting text into those pieces. It is like breaking words into syllables, except the pieces are chosen by statistics.

A model only works with the tokenizer it was trained with; mixing them produces gibberish. The tokenizer files ship inside the model's repository and the engine loads them automatically. You rarely set one by hand, except for the few models that borrow another model's tokenizer.

tool_calling.title: Tool calling (function calling)
tool_calling.short: The model asks the application to run a function, such as a search, by writing a structured request.
tool_calling.long:
In tool calling you describe functions to the model (name, purpose, arguments). Instead of answering, the model may reply with a request like 'call get_weather with city = Oslo'.

Your application runs the function and sends the result back. Models write these requests in their own formats, so the engine needs the matching 'tool-call parser' to turn the text into the standard API shape. Without the right parser, agents and coding tools see raw text, get no tool calls and stall.

top_p.title: Top-p (nucleus sampling)
top_p.short: A setting that limits word choices to the most likely tokens whose probabilities add up to p.
top_p.long: With top-p 0.9 the engine sorts the candidate tokens by probability, keeps the smallest set that together covers 90%, and chooses among those. Unlikely oddities in the long tail are never picked. It works alongside temperature: temperature changes the shape of the probabilities and top-p cuts off the tail. Change one at a time, and start from the pair of values on the model card.

torch_compile.title: torch.compile
torch_compile.short: PyTorch's compiler, which fuses many small operations into fewer, faster ones.
torch_compile.long: torch.compile analyses the model's code and generates optimised GPU kernels. The first start with a new model, engine version or setting can spend minutes compiling. Later starts reuse the cached result, which is why the console gives some engines a cache volume that survives restarts. It usually makes inference somewhat faster. When it fails or hangs, switching it off is a common workaround.

trust_remote_code.title: Trust remote code
trust_remote_code.short: A switch that lets the engine run Python code taken from the model's repository, and is off unless you set it.
trust_remote_code.long:
Some new model designs are not yet built into the engine, so the model's repository ships the Python code that implements them. 'Trust remote code' lets the engine download and run that code inside its container.

It is exactly as risky as running a stranger's program: the code can read everything the container can read, such as prompts and mounted files. The internal network keeps it from sending data out, but do not enable it for repositories you have not reviewed. If a model refuses to load until it is on, wait for built-in support or read the code first.

ttft.title: Time to first token (TTFT)
ttft.short: How long you wait after sending a request before the first word of the answer appears.
ttft.long: TTFT is the time spent waiting in line plus the time to read the prompt (prefill). For a short prompt on an idle engine it is usually a fraction of a second. For a long prompt it grows with the prompt's length, and when the engine is overloaded it grows with the queue. The console reports the median (p50: half of the requests are faster) and p95 (only one request in twenty is slower). A big gap between the two means some requests wait much longer than typical.

unified_memory.title: Unified memory
unified_memory.short: A design where the GPU and the CPU share one pool of memory, so there is no separate VRAM.
unified_memory.long: Most computers have two memory pools: RAM for the CPU and VRAM for the GPU. Some machines, such as systems built on NVIDIA's GB10 chip, use a single pool for both. That makes large models possible on a small box, but the model, the KV cache and the operating system now compete for the same memory, and that memory is usually slower than the VRAM of a big graphics card. The console treats such a machine as one budget: VRAM use and RAM use are added together.

vision_language_model.title: Vision-language model (VLM)
vision_language_model.short: A model that accepts images together with text and answers in text.
vision_language_model.long: A vision-language model has an image encoder in front of the language model. Each image is turned into many tokens, often hundreds to thousands depending on its size, so pictures use up context window and KV cache quickly. Engines accept images through the same chat API, usually as links or inline data, and have settings that limit how many images one prompt may contain. Not all engines support all vision models.

vllm.title: vLLM
vllm.short: An open-source engine for serving language models to many users at once, with paged attention and continuous batching.
vllm.long: vLLM loads models in Hugging Face format (safetensors) and supports a wide range of quantization formats and multi-GPU layouts. Its server speaks the OpenAI-compatible API, publishes Prometheus metrics, and can serve LoRA adapters, vision models and speculative decoding. It runs in a container image whose version decides which models and settings work, so check the image tag when a new model fails to load.

vram.title: VRAM (GPU memory)
vram.short: The graphics card's own memory, in which the weights, the KV cache and working buffers must all fit.
vram.long:
VRAM (video RAM) is much faster than a machine's normal RAM and much smaller: from about 8 GB in small cards to 96 GB or more in workstation and data-centre cards. Think of VRAM as the workbench and ordinary RAM as the storeroom down the corridor: the work happens on the bench, and every trip to the storeroom costs time.

An engine fills it with three things: the weights (fixed size), the KV cache (grows with conversation length and with the number of users) and working buffers for the calculations. When they add up to more than the card holds, the engine stops with an 'out of memory' error. VRAM cannot be extended like a disk. If a model does not fit, use a smaller or more compressed one, shorten the context, or spread the model over more GPUs.

warmup.title: Warm-up
warmup.short: The work an engine does after loading, before it is fully fast: compiling kernels and recording CUDA graphs.
warmup.long: Loading the weights is only part of start-up. The engine then tries out dummy batches, compiles code for your GPU and records CUDA graphs, which can take from a few seconds to many minutes the first time. The console shows these phases while the instance is loading. Later starts are faster because compiled code is cached. Even when the engine says ready, the very first requests may still be slower than later ones.

weights.title: Weights
weights.short: The learned numbers inside a model, which take up most of the memory a model needs.
weights.long:
Training adjusts billions of numbers until the model does its job well. Those numbers are the weights. They are stored in files (safetensors or GGUF) and must be loaded into GPU memory before the model can answer anything.

How much room they take depends on how many there are and how precisely each one is stored: 2 bytes each in bf16, 1 byte in fp8, about half a byte in 4-bit formats. A 70-billion-parameter model is about 140 GB in bf16, 70 GB in fp8 and roughly 40 GB in a 4-bit format. The weights do not change while an engine runs. The part of memory that does change with traffic is the KV cache.

yarn.title: YaRN
yarn.short: 'Yet another RoPE extension': a popular RoPE scaling method for stretching a model to a longer context.
yarn.long: YaRN adjusts the position numbers in a way that keeps short-range accuracy better than simple stretching. A typical use is to run a model trained for 32,000 tokens at 128,000 (a factor of 4). In many engines the setting is static: it applies to every request, long or short, so short prompts may lose a little quality. Longer context also needs more KV cache, so check the fit before you launch.

zfs.title: ZFS
zfs.short: A file system that pools disks and keeps its own read cache in RAM, which changes how memory figures look.
zfs.long: ZFS combines several disks into a pool, with snapshots and checksums. It caches data in its own memory (the ARC) instead of the normal page cache. On a ZFS host, memory tools therefore show that cache as used memory, not as cache, and it is released back under pressure, within limits. This can make 'available' RAM look lower than on a machine with ordinary disks. The console shows a pool's name and type in a model's drive label.
